en: Sutta Nipāta 4.3 Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasutta:
"Indeed, some who are ill-disposed say:"
Furthermore, they speak with truthful minds;
yet the Sage does not enter into arisen disputes.
Therefore, for the Sage, there is no obstruction anywhere.
For how could one overcome his own view when he is led by desire,
settled in his own preference,
and acting according to his own convictions?
For one should speak exactly as one knows.
A person who proclaims their own virtuous conduct to others without being asked—
The wise call that ignoble state (anariyadhamma) by which one brings ruin upon oneself;
whereas the virtuous bhikkhu is one whose self is fully extinguished.
They destroy it by not being boastful regarding their virtues;
the wise call that the noble dhamma for one who has no conceit anywhere in the world.
For one whose mental states are fabricated and conditioned,
who is preoccupied with things that are not pure—
when he perceives within himself a benefit [in those things], [he is lost].
Relying on that unstable peace dependent [on conditions],
one has not transcended the settling into views;
for among phenomena, one has merely grasped what was selected.
Therefore, a person, amidst those dwellings,
neither rejects nor grasps at phenomena;
for the one who is cleansed has nothing whatsoever anywhere in the world.
Having abandoned views conceived regarding various states of existence,
and having cast off illusion and pride,
the one who is free from acquisitions— by what means could he go anywhere?
For one who employs means enters into debate regarding phenomena;
how could one who is without means speak?
For him, there is neither self nor non-self.
"He has shaken off every view right here"—
this was the third sutta, the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka*.
